summary: LSP-Ping cannot verify connectivity of a segment of a multi-segment pseudowire or bidirectional co-routed LSP from any node along the path. This document defines a Time to Live TLV to address that shortcoming.

plainLanguage.summary: A traceroute-style check lets you test only part of a long path. This RFC adds a counter to a ping message so you can test from the middle of a route.

questions: what is the lsp ping ttl tlv
how does lsp ping reply ttl work
subtitle: A small optional field in an MPLS echo request that tells the far end how many hops back to send its reply.

tldr.problem: LSP-Ping could not verify a segment of a multi-segment pseudowire or a bidirectional co-routed LSP from a node in the middle of the path, because the replier did not know how many hops away the originator was.
tldr.mechanism: The originator adds a Time To Live TLV to its MPLS Echo Request. The TLV carries the hop count, and the receiver uses it as the TTL on the MPLS header of its Echo Reply so the reply expires at the originator.
tldr.outcome: Any node on the path can now test connectivity to another node on it. The scope is limited to MS-PWs and bidirectional co-routed LSPs, where the reply travels back along the same path.

today: RFC 7394 is a Proposed Standard from November 2014. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: The Problem: Replying to a Mid-Path Originator
sections.content:
LSP-Ping is an Operation, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) mechanism in MPLS networks. A node sends an MPLS Echo Request and gets back an MPLS Echo Reply. A multi-segment pseudowire (MS-PW) can span several service provider networks, and providers want to check segments of it from any node on the path, not just from the ends.

If the originator sits at the end of the MS-PW, the receiver can reply without knowing the hop distance, because the end node intercepts the reply whatever its TTL is. If the originator is in the middle, the receiver may need to know how many hops away it is so that it can set the TTL on the MPLS header of the reply and have the reply intercepted at the originator. The same need arises on bidirectional co-routed LSPs.

The RFC defines a new optional TTL TLV for this. The originator adds it to the Echo Request to say how many hops away it is.
sections.plainLanguage: If you shout to a friend from the middle of a long hallway, your friend does not know how far to send the answer back. Telling them the distance fixes that.

sections.title: The TTL TLV Format
sections.content:
The TLV has a Type of 32769 and a Length of 8. Its body holds a Value field (the TTL to use), a Reserved field and a 16-bit Flags field.

One flag is defined, the R flag (Reply TTL). It signals that the value is meant to be used as the TTL for the reply packet. All other flag bits are Reserved: they MUST be zero when sending and are ignored on receipt. The RFC notes that other bits may be defined later to widen the scope of the TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: The note has a small label saying what kind of note it is, a number for the distance, and a tick box meaning use this number for the reply.

sections.title: How Senders and Receivers Use the TLV
sections.content:
The originator MAY include the TTL TLV in the MPLS Echo Request. It is optional, so a receiver that does not understand it ignores it, as with any optional TLV. If the TLV is absent or not processed, how the reply's TTL gets chosen is outside the scope of the document.

If the receiver understands the TLV, one of two things happens:

  • If the value field is zero, the echo request SHOULD be dropped.
  • Otherwise the receiver MUST use the value from the TLV when it builds the MPLS header of the Echo Reply. This value takes precedence over any TTL determined by other means, such as the Switching Point TLV in the MS-PW. That precedence helps the originator analyse the return path.

The mechanism only works if the reply goes back down the co-routed LSP. The presence of the TLV implies use of the co-routed return path. If the return path uses any other mechanism, the TLV in the request MUST be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: If the receiver knows about the distance number, it uses it. If the number is zero, it just throws the note away. If it does not know about the number, it ignores it.

sections.title: An Example and Traceroute Mode
sections.content:
Take an MS-PW running through LSRs A, B, C, D and E. An operator wants to check connectivity from B to D. B sends an Echo Request carrying the TTL TLV towards D, with the request containing the FEC of the PW segment between C and D. Both the TLV value and the TTL in the MPLS label are set to 2. The value can come from operator input or from the optional LDP switching point TLV.

The request is intercepted at D because its TTL expires. D sees the TTL TLV and puts the value 2 on the MPLS label of its Echo Reply, which expires at B and is intercepted there. The same procedure works for a co-routed bidirectional LSP between an intermediate LSR B and another LSR D.

In traceroute mode the TLV value is set to 1 for the first Echo Request, then 2 for the next, and so on, similar to the TTL values used for the label on the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Like a traceroute game: first you shout to the kid one step away, then two steps away, then three, and each answer comes back the right distance.

sections.title: The Error Scenario and Return TTL
sections.content:
An Echo Request can be intercepted before its intended destination, for example because of network faults or misconfiguration, rather than because the label TTL expired. If the reply then used the full TLV value as its TTL, it would continue beyond the originating node, which the RFC calls a security issue.

To prevent this, the label TTL on the Echo Reply MUST be reduced by the incoming label TTL on the received packet. If the request is punted to the CPU before the incoming label TTL is deducted, another 1 MUST be added. In short:

Return TTL = (TTL TLV Value) - (Incoming Label TTL) + 1
sections.plainLanguage: If the note gets stopped early, the answer should not fly past you. So the receiver subtracts the steps the note already skipped, and the answer stops where it should.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the TLV lets the sender choose the TTL of the reply's MPLS label, a device could receive many LSP-Ping packets redirected to its CPU. The RFC says this is possible without the changes too, and that a device should rate limit LSP-Ping packets redirected to the CPU.

The advice in RFC 4379 to check the source address of the Echo Request still applies, except that the source can now be any node along the LSP path. A faulty transit node that alters the TLV value could make the wrong node reply, or the wrong node receive the reply. An LSP trace may help find such a node.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could flood a router with test notes, so routers should only answer so many per second.

sections.title: IANA Allocation
sections.content: IANA assigned the Time To Live TLV a type value from the TLVs subregistry of the MPLS LSPs Ping Parameters registry. The value allocated is 32769.
sections.plainLanguage: The new note type got its own official number so everyone recognises it.

fields.name: Value
fields.desc: The TTL to use on the reply.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Only the R (Reply TTL) bit is defined; the rest MUST be zero.
